one_liner: TypeScript prime-field library whose AssemblyScript WASM backend runs 128-bit vector field ops about 9x faster than its JS BigInt path.
what_it_does: Finite-field arithmetic for Node.js: scalar ops on bigint plus immutable Vector and Matrix types with element-wise arithmetic, matrix products, polynomial add/mul/div, FFT evaluation and interpolation over roots of unity, Lagrange and batched quartic interpolation, and Montgomery batch inversion (algorithms largely copied from Vitalik Buterin's MIMC STARK code). createPrimeField(modulus, true) returns a WASM-backed field only when the modulus lies between 2^128 - 2^64 and 2^128, and silently falls back to the JS BigInt field otherwise. The API is the library's own FiniteField interface, not a drop-in for any other package.
how_it_is_fast: Vector and matrix elements live in WebAssembly linear memory as two u64 limbs each, and the AssemblyScript kernel (lib/assembly/prime128.as.ts, built with asc -O3) loops over them without allocating a JS BigInt per result. Modular multiplication is an unrolled two-iteration word-by-word reduction that estimates the quotient as z >> 128, which works because the modulus is 2^128 - k with k < 2^64; 64x64-bit products are assembled from 32-bit halves since WASM has no wide multiply. Exponentiation is square-and-multiply and inversion is binary extended GCD, both in WASM.
when_to_use: Node.js STARK or polynomial-commitment prototypes that work in a 128-bit prime field of the form 2^128 - k (k < 2^64) and process vectors of thousands to hundreds of thousands of elements.
Bulk element-wise add/sub/mul/exp, matrix products, FFT-based evaluation and interpolation where data can stay in WASM vectors between calls.
You already use the JS BigInt field of this library and want the roughly 8.8x (add, mul) to 9.2x (exp) vector speedup by passing useWasm or a WebAssembly.Memory.
Short-lived processes or flows that create a bounded number of vectors, since WASM memory is never released.
when_not_to_use: Scalar arithmetic: WasmPrimeField128.add/mul/exp/inv on single bigints delegate to the JS BigInt field, so per-element call patterns get no speedup.
256-bit or other moduli (for example BN254 or BLS12-381 scalar fields): no WASM path exists (issue #9 open since 2019), and the README's 256-bit column is plain BigInt.
Long-running services: WASM memory used by vectors and matrices is never freed (README note, issue #10 open since 2019), so fields must be re-created periodically.
Browsers without a bundler shim: the loader reads prime128.wasm with fs.readFileSync and __dirname (issue #29 'Building for browser?' is unanswered).
Secret-dependent cryptographic code: the maintainer says to assume nothing is constant time (issue #13), and the WASM modAdd/modMul still branch on zero operands and on comparisons.

integration.form: module (npm package @guildofweavers/galois 0.4.22, compiled TypeScript plus prime128.wasm)
integration.dependencies: @assemblyscript/loader 0.8.x at runtime; AssemblyScript 0.8.x, TypeScript, gulp and mocha to build
integration.min_toolchain: Node.js 12.7 or newer (package.json engines; needs BigInt and BigUint64Array); WASM bulk-memory support
integration.platforms: Node.js (any CPU V8 runs on); browser use not supported out of the box
integration.thread_safety: not documented; each field instance owns one WASM instance with shared input/output scratch buffers and no locking
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same FiniteField API as the library's JS BigInt field, enabled by a flag, but only for moduli in (2^128 - 2^64, 2^128), and Vector/Matrix objects from a JS field cannot be passed to WASM-field methods (they are cast to WasmVector128 without checks)

gotchas: Harness flaw behind the README table: tests/benchmarks.ts times one pass of 2^18 elements per operation with Date.now() (1 ms resolution), no warm-up or repetition, JS section first; the 44M additions/s figure corresponds to a single interval of about 6 ms (derived: 262,144 / 44M), so plus or minus 1 ms is about 17%. The WASM timings exclude copying inputs into WASM memory (timed separately) and never copy results back, the benchmark pre-allocates a 256 MB WebAssembly.Memory where the default is 10 pages that grow on demand, and the 256-bit JS section is commented out (and calls f1.divVectorElements on 256-bit vectors), so the 256-bit column cannot be regenerated.

WasmVector128.load and setValue do not reduce inputs mod p: setValue only rejects values above 2^128 - 1 and load silently splits any bigint into two u64 words, while the WASM kernels assume canonical elements below the modulus; pass only reduced, non-negative values.
The modulus is not validated as prime (issue #5 open), and the README example uses a 256-bit modulus that gets no WASM acceleration.

The maintainer said in issue #11 (Aug 2019) that enabling -O3 made no noticeable difference; the arrayElementOp loop dispatches each element through a function-pointer call, so the kernel is not inlined.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick galois over long.js (64-bit integers with a WASM multiply/divide fast path) or berith (fixed Ed25519/X25519 curves) when you need general prime-field vector, matrix and FFT polynomial arithmetic in a 2^128 - k field on Node; for any other field size or a browser target none of these fits and a maintained library is the better choice.
verified_claims_summary: On an Intel Core i5-7300U, single thread, Node.js version unstated, the README reports rounded element-wise ops/s for the library's 128-bit WASM field against its own JS BigInt field: additions 44.0M vs 5.0M, multiplications 16.3M vs 1.85M, exponentiations 97,000 vs 10,500 (about 8.8x, 8.8x and 9.2x, derived from page data); the 256-bit BigInt column is lower still (3.2M, 0.95M, 3,200). The numbers come from one Date.now() pass over 2^18-element vectors in tests/benchmarks.ts, which checks every WASM result against the JS result; AssemblyScript 0.8.x with asc -O3.
status_note: Abandoned: last code change 2022-05-22 (a merged PR adding binomial support to interpolateRoots), the substantive work dates from 2019, 8 open issues and 18 open PRs sit unanswered, and it is pinned to AssemblyScript 0.8.x; MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor if you can live with the WASM memory leak.
